summary: Defines the part of the Management Information Base used for managing OSPF version 2, the Open Shortest Path First routing protocol. It was a draft standard and was replaced by RFC 4750.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of dials and readings letting a person check and control how a router is doing its path-finding.

questions: how to manage ospf with snmp
subtitle: Management objects for monitoring and controlling OSPF version 2 routing protocol routers.

tldr.problem: Network operators running OSPF version 2 routing protocol needed a standard way to monitor and manage OSPF routers using SNMP, with objects for configuring areas, interfaces, neighbors, and tracking routing calculations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1850 defines a comprehensive MIB using SMIv2 that organizes OSPF data into groups: general variables (router ID, version, AS border status), areas with stub metric tables, the link state database, interfaces with metrics, virtual interfaces, neighbor relationships, and external route information. It includes support for demand routing and multicast extensions.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now remotely view and configure OSPF router state, SPF calculation statistics, neighbor relationships, interface parameters, and area structure. This RFC improved upon RFC 1253 with support for new OSPF features and was itself replaced by RFC 4750.

today: RFC 1850 was a draft standard for managing OSPF version 2. It was obsoleted by RFC 4750, which provides updated MIB definitions for OSPF as the protocol and network management practices evolved.

sections.title: OSPF Routing and Management
sections.content:
Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is an interior gateway routing protocol that routers use to exchange reachability information within an autonomous system. Unlike distance-vector protocols that only exchange hop counts, OSPF routers distribute detailed link-state information and run the Dijkstra algorithm to compute shortest paths. To manage OSPF deployments, network operators need standard ways to query router state, configure areas and interfaces, and monitor routing calculations.

RFC 1850 replaces RFC 1253 with an updated MIB using SMIv2, adding support for NSSA areas, demand routing extensions, multicast forwarding capabilities, and improved handling of external routes and area aggregates. The MIB is organized into logical sections covering global OSPF parameters, area configuration, link state databases, interfaces, neighbors, and traps.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF is how routers tell each other about all the paths in a network and pick the best ones. This RFC describes how to ask an OSPF router what it knows and how to change its settings.

sections.title: MIB Organization and Core Data Structures
sections.content:
The MIB consists of several major sections. The General Variables group defines global parameters: the router ID (a 32-bit identifier, typically an IP address), administrative status (enabled or disabled), OSPF version number, area border router status, AS border router status, counters for external LSAs, support for type-of-service routing, and demand routing extensions.

The Area Table describes each OSPF area the router participates in. Each area is identified by a 32-bit area ID; area 0.0.0.0 is the backbone. Area entries include authentication type, whether external routes are imported, the count of SPF algorithm runs, counts of area border routers and AS border routers reachable within the area, the number of LSAs in the area database, and the checksum sum of LSAs for database verification.

Additional tables cover stub area metrics, the link state database (excluding external LSAs), address ranges, host routes, interface configurations, virtual links, neighbor relationships, and external link state advertisements. Each table relates to a specific aspect of OSPF operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is organized like file folders: one for global settings, one for each area, one showing what networks the router knows about, one for each network interface, and one for each neighbor router.

sections.title: Interface Configuration and Metrics
sections.content:
The Interface Table defines per-interface parameters including the interface index, area the interface belongs to, interface type (broadcast, point-to-point, NBMA, virtual, or point-to-multipoint), state (down, waiting, point-to-point, designated router, backup designated router, or other), router priority (used in designated router election), designated router address, backup designated router address, and authentication key.

Timers are configurable per interface: the Hello interval (default 10 seconds), Dead interval (default 40 seconds), retransmission interval (default 5 seconds), and transit delay (default 1 second). The Interface Metrics Table holds the cost metric for each type-of-service on each interface. This separation allows different metrics for different TOS levels, with the default TOS 0 metric calculated intelligently from interface speed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each interface has settings like 'say hello every 10 seconds' and a cost saying how good this path is. The cost might be fast or slow depending on the link speed.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and Virtual Links
sections.content:
The Neighbor Table lists all OSPF neighbors discovered on the router's interfaces. Each neighbor entry shows the neighbor's router ID, the interface on which the neighbor is reachable, neighbor state (down, attempt, init, two-way, exchange-start, exchange, loading, or full), neighbor router priority, neighbor designated router status, and event counters (hello packets received, database description packets, link state requests, and link state updates).

The table also includes retransmission counters, the last time the neighbor sent an event, and whether the neighbor is permanently configured (for NBMA networks) or dynamically learned. For NBMA interfaces, neighbors must be manually configured before OSPF Hello packets can be exchanged.

The Virtual Interface Table describes virtual links across non-backbone areas. A virtual link connects the backbone to a transit area when the backbone is disconnected, or connects an area without a direct backbone connection. Virtual links are configured by specifying the remote router ID and the transit area ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps a list of neighbor routers it talks to, their status, and counters for packets exchanged. For fake network links (virtual links), it remembers which distant router and area they connect.

sections.title: SPF Calculation and Database Management
sections.content:
The ospfSpfRuns counter in the area table tracks how many times the Shortest Path First algorithm has executed for that area, typically using Dijkstra's algorithm to recompute the routing tree when the topology changes. This counter helps operators understand routing stability; frequent SPF runs can indicate a flapping link or unstable network.

The Link State Database Table displays all LSAs (Link State Advertisements) in the router's database for quick inspection during troubleshooting. Each entry shows the LSA type (router LSA, network LSA, summary LSA, summary ASBR LSA, external LSA, etc.), the advertising router ID, the LSA sequence number, age, and checksum. The database checksum sum allows quick verification that two routers have identical databases.

The External Link State Database (added to separate it from regular LSAs) shows external routes injected into OSPF from other routing sources. Operators can configure aggregation of external routes and control whether external routes are imported into stub areas.
sections.plainLanguage: The router counts how many times it recalculated its map of the network. It keeps a detailed database of every link advertised by every router. For routes from outside OSPF, it has a separate list.

sections.title: Operational Control and Area Types
sections.content:
The MIB supports multiple area types. Regular areas receive all types of routes. Stub areas do not contain external routes and instead rely on a default route to reach external networks, reducing the size of the link state database. Totally stubby areas receive only a default route. NSSA areas (Not So Stubby Areas) can import external routes but still block most external routes from other areas.

The ospfImportAsExtern object controls whether a router imports external routes into each area (importExternal), excludes them (importNoExternal), or uses NSSA behavior. The ospfAreaSummary object controls whether a stub area border router advertises summary LSAs or only a default route.

For demand routing, the ospfDemandExtensions object enables periodic hello suppression when the topology is stable, useful for reducing traffic on dial-up or switched circuits. The ospfMulticastExtensions object enables multicast routing extensions in 3 bits: intra-area multicasting, inter-area multicasting, and inter-AS multicasting.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can configure different types of areas to reduce the amount of routing information routers need to keep. They can also enable faster hellos or reduce unnecessary messages on expensive links.
